title: How Your Hobbies Can Make You A Better Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Citing David Epstein's book Range, Linsin argues that a wide range of interests outside teaching, not deeper immersion in instructional methods, is what makes teachers most effective. He contends that content knowledge and lived experience—drawn from hobbies like travel, sports, or the arts—give teachers the personal anecdotes and enthusiasm needed to bring subject matter to life and pull students into a state of flow. He warns that overfocusing on instructional technique at the expense of outside interests can actually make teachers worse, since methods can be learned quickly while genuine expertise and passion cannot be faked. His concluding advice is straightforward: pursue hobbies and outside interests without guilt, both as an antidote to burnout and as a path to becoming a more compelling teacher.
points: Cites research from David Epstein's book Range showing Nobel laureates are far more likely than peers to have outside hobbies.

quotes: In David Epstein’s recent book Range, he makes the case that most breakthroughs in science, art, technology, medicine, music, and sports come from those with a wide range of interests and abilities.
For example, Nobel laureates in science are 22 times more likely than their peers to have hobbies outside of their field.

Your deep understanding of content is what draws students in and causes them to care about what they’re learning. It’s the stories, the personalities, the little-known history and inside-baseball that inspire students to want to learn.
Making teaching your hobby or primary interest—as so many teachers do—can actually make you a worse teacher.
Get away from teaching. Go hiking with your family. Swim. Paint. Read. Write. Play an instrument. Start a business. Take a class. Coach your kid’s soccer team.
Not only is it a powerful antidote to teaching-related stress, but you’ll become a more effective, interesting, and charismatic teacher.
